This means building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms that allow risk to be distributed across a broader set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool of global capital to development opportunities. question: On current trajectories, how many jobs are developing countries expected to generate while 1.2 billion young people reach working age?
answer: On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to generate only about 420 million jobs while 1.2 billion young people reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years [wbg-ar-2026:p005:para1000:000, wbg-ar-2026:p007:para1000:001].

When we create jobs, we strengthen economic and social stability, reduce mass migration, improve livelihoods, enhance resilience to economic shocks, and prevent people from falling back into poverty. That benefits everyone, everywhere.

With 1.2 billion young people reaching working age in the next 10 to 15 years, the need for more and better-paid jobs is more urgent than ever. On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to generate only about 420 million jobs over that same period — leaving a gap of staggering proportions. Jobs are created when firms can operate reliably, plan with confidence, and invest with reasonable expectations of return. Our strategy reflects that reality:

• First, invest in foundational physical and human infrastructure;

• Second, support a business-enabling environment with clear rules and regulations;

• And third, mobilize private capital at scale.

Ajay Banga

President of the World Bank Group Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors

JOBS ARE ESSENTIAL. THEY PROVIDE DIGNITY, HOPE, AND BELIEF IN A BETTER FUTURE. When jobs are created at scale, they strengthen communities, transform countries, and power the global economy.

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing countries. Those countries are expected to create only about 420 million jobs. Whether this generation becomes an engine of growth or a source of instability will depend in large part on whether they can find productive work.

That is why creating jobs is the overarching focus of the World Bank Group. Three years ago, our shareholders and clients gave us a clear mandate: build a better and bigger World Bank Group — faster, simpler, and better able to bring private capital alongside our own financing and knowledge.

Built around four pillars — mobilizing private capital, expanding equity investments, revamping support for small- and medium-size businesses, and reinforcing coordination across the World Bank Group — we are strengthening our ability to support the businesses and entrepreneurs needed to create employment opportunities in developing countries. The business, operational, and thematic highlights that follow demonstrate how IFC’s evolving model is translating into concrete outcomes for clients, investors, and communities in the countries it serves.

This year’s results show the progress we have made. We delivered $123.5 billion in financing to clients. We mobilized $112 billion in private capital, more than triple the $35 billion we mobilized in fiscal 2022. Disputes are decided by an arbitral tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members are typically appointed by the parties from among international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides administrative services for arbitrations conducted under UNCITRAL and other non-ICSID frameworks. Fiscal 2026 was a record year for ICSID. The Centre administered 363 cases — the highest in its history — up from 347 in fiscal 2025 and 341 in fiscal 2024. [wbg-ar-2026:p043:para1000:007 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 43]
During fiscal 2026, ICSID registered 60 new cases — 57 arbitrations under the ICSID Convention and three under the Additional Facility Rules — bringing the cumulative total to 1,118 registered cases as of June 30, 2026. On the mediation front, ICSID had received a total of seven requests under Mediation Rule 6 and Mediation Rule 5, with one proceeding administered as of fiscal 2026. The year also saw 83 proceedings concluded, marking the third consecutive fiscal year in which conclusions surpassed 80.

Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among disputes decided by tribunals in the past year, 37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full, 40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

Key findings show that contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more time-efficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus 34 percent. The paper is accompanied by a special issue of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics featuring data on contract-based cases.
